item.title: The Rise of the Lonely Engineer
item.description:
In my post about multinational teams I wrote that a colleague’s silence in a meeting could mean at least six different things. They might be thinking deeply, disagreeing strongly, waiting to be invited to speak, fighting a bad connection, processing in a second language or just really needing coffee.

I missed one. There is a seventh meaning now. They are talking to their agent.

Nobody asks me “hey, do you have five minutes?” as often as they used to. The questions didn’t go away. They went somewhere else. The somewhere else never gets tired, never needs coffee and never says “I have no idea, let’s ask someone else.”

I’ve complained before that AI turned me into a project manager for a machine. This post is about the other side of that deal. When everyone has a sidekick, what happens to the team?

item.title: We Got Tricked Into Writing Documentation
item.description:
I didn’t sign up to be a project manager. I got into programming because I loved the exploration, making mistakes, finding solutions and moving slowly bit by bit. One day I needed system tool then I wrote some C, the other time I needed some glue code, so I got comfortable with Perl or Bash. Needed to created website? Well… PHP was the languge for it - basically whatever was up to the job. I never learned any of these to the level of a professional, was never interested.

I’ve enjoyed solving puzzles, one at the time, it was creative freeform craft. It was messy, it was dounting. It was fun, sooo much fun!

Now I spend my days writing prose about code instead.

Kent Beck calls AI code agents the genie in the bottle: you get what you wish for, not what you want. He’s right, but in ways I did not expected.
